//: The boundary of the certified item: which kernel source files and which
library crates are inside the thing a certificate would attach to, which
are the uncertified load above it, and which are verification rather
than product.
Enforced by tools/common/check/check-item-boundary.py and explained in
docs/certification/ITEM.md. Every assurance artifact in docs/certification
is scoped to this file: the Security Target's TOE, the hazard analysis's
safety item, the traceability matrix and the coverage obligation all mean
'the rings named here'. Move a file between rings and you have changed
what four ratings are claims about, which is why it is a diff somebody has
to argue for rather than a directory convention.
Three rings, nested, tightest first. The point of the nesting is that the
boundary can ratchet inward without re-scoping the scheme: raising the
target from EAL5+ to EAL6+, or from SIL 2 to ASIL D, is then a matter of
moving modules from 'item' to 'core', not of rewriting the artifacts.
A file in no ring fails the build. That is the ratchet's teeth: a new
kernel module cannot drift into the item by being written, and cannot
drift out of the analysis by being forgotten. Library crates are
classified whole, under `crates` below.
A certificate attaches to a configuration, not to a repository. This is
the one under evaluation: the `present` kernel profile
(tools/common/data/profiles/present.toml, docs/BUILD-FLAGS.md BF1), on
three architectures, release profile, the gate set cargo xtask check
runs, and the toolchain rust-toolchain.toml pins. Seven Cargo features
exist in the whole workspace and none is in src/kernel/ or
src/boot/common/uefi/, so there is no Cargo configuration space to
enumerate -- which is most of why this item is analysable at all.
The kernel's configuration is its build flags (build-flags.toml): each
chosen at compile time as `cfg(ferrix_<flag> = "<value>")`, set only by
xtask from a profile file, read only in the kernel crate, and printed by
the kernel on its `build` boot line, which the gate compares with the
profile. `present` sets every one; a build changed by `--set` is ad hoc
and carries no claim. `mitigations=off`, `checks=off` and `linux_abi=off`
(LINUX-ABI-SEPARATION.md 11.11, build-only) are such builds.
`cargo xtask check` type-checks (clippy, no link) the kernel in every
buildable profile, checks=off, mitigations=off and linux_abi=off on every architecture
so none can rot; `cargo xtask test-flags` links and boots each buildable
profile, and `test-boot --mitigations off --no-claim` the off build.
check-item-boundary.py holds the values below to present.toml's.
devmgr_why: One boot option changes what the item does: `ferrix.devmgr=kernel|init`
(docs/INIT.md 7.3, L12). `kernel`, the default and the reference, has the
kernel start devmgr at bring-up, run the disk checks of stages 10 to 12
through its drivers, and switch / before pid 1. `init` has pid 1 start
devmgr through a one-shot starter, skips those checks, switches / after
devmgr has reported, and re-roots pid 1 with the switch. It exists, the
images that boot /sbin/init use it, and no claim is made of it
pstore_why: A second boot option changes what the item does: `ferrix.pstore=on|off`
(docs/POSTMORTEM.md 3). `on`, the default and the reference, has the
loader give the kernel one region of RAM, which the kernel checks and
mirrors its log into, and writes back at the end of a panic report; the
next boot's loader reports what survived. Every stop on purpose records
how in the header's stop word and writes the region back (docs/POSTMORTEM.md
5), so the next loader says how the boot ended. `off`, or any other value,
said, takes no region. Claims: L.console.42-44, L.console.46-48 and L.mm.75;
the record is a diagnostic only (SAFETY-MANUAL AoU-30, VULNERABILITY-ANALYSIS
efifb_why: `ferrix.efifb` lends the boot framebuffer to a ring-3 driver, efifb,
on x86-64 (docs/DISPLAY.md 8; L.device.38-42): stage 10 publishes one
more node whose aperture is the framebuffer's visible lines, the one
exemption from the reserved ranges, and leaves the PCI function that
holds it undriven. `off`, the default and the reference, adds no node.
`on` is the firmware-screen boot's and a GPU-less PC's, and no claim is
made of it (ITEM.md 5, SAFETY-MANUAL AoU-31; the certification
panic_why: `ferrix.panic=reset` (H.FAIL.5) resets the machine 10 s after a
panic's report: a stop-gap for the N150 box, set by no loader, outside
the claim. `halt`, the default and the reference, is the safe state
H.FAIL.1 and SAFETY-MANUAL 3 claim; any other value is said and taken
vtd_why: `ferrix.vtd=off` leaves every VT-d unit alone (L.iommu.71): no DMA is
translated, no interrupt remapped, the isolated-interrupts mark is
refused, and the audit record's Vtd configuration item reads 0. `on`,
the default and the reference, drives every unit accept takes; any
other value is driven as `on`. `off` is for recovering a machine whose
units break its boot, outside the reference configuration (ITEM.md 5,
SAFETY-MANUAL AoU-8; the certification consultant's ledger 2026-10-17,
driver_updates_why: Whether the image carries drvupdated, the helper through which root
puts a new driver image on a device while the machine runs
(docs/DEVMGR.md 4.1). It changes no kernel code: devmgr and every
driver stay outside the item, and a replaced driver is the T.DMA
attacker already, confined by the same domain, quiesce and quarantine.
But a driver image after boot is not authenticated until the update's
verification lands (D3). `absent`, the reference, is every image but
`test-restart --update`'s, and xtask refuses any other image that
carries the helper (native::refuse_updater). `test` is those images
alone, and no claim is made of them (ITEM.md 5, SAFETY-MANUAL AoU-26;

//: The levels, the flags and each value's levels are defined once, in
the flag file (docs/BUILD-FLAGS.md BF2), and each profile in its own
file; this manifest names them rather than copying them. Each ring
above carries its `level`, the level its components are certified
at: core and item at `present` (today's four targets), the load at
`none`, linked into ring 0 only when `in_ring0_when` holds, which in
`present` is by the dated exception that ends at M5's flip. A crate
may name a `level` of its own. check-item-boundary.py's profile rule
requires every component a profile links into ring 0 to be at the
profile's level or above (rule 3), standard by standard.

//test_file_patterns: In-kernel self-tests: the code behind 'every boot proves its own claims'.
Product code and verification code are counted apart everywhere in the
assurance argument, because a standard asks quite different questions of
each -- the first has to be covered by tests, the second *is* the test.
Roughly a quarter of src/kernel/ is this. Excluding it from the item's size
is not a way of looking smaller: these files are cited as verification
evidence in docs/certification/VERIFICATION.md, where they have to earn

core.status: aspirational -- the ratchet's destination, not a current claim
why: The minimal trusted computing base: the code that must be correct for
memory protection, scheduling and capability enforcement to mean
anything. Nothing here may depend on a filesystem, a network stack or
a device driver, and that is checked rather than intended.
This ring is what a later EAL6+ or ASIL D effort would evaluate. It is
named now, while it is cheap to name, because the cost of discovering
a boundary later is every artifact written against the wrong one.

item.status: the boundary the current artifacts are written against
why: The core, plus the code that brings it up, dispatches into it and
enumerates the hardware it hands to ring 3. This is the item all four
present ratings attach to.
The native ABI is here rather than in the core because it is the
interface the item exports, and an interface is evaluated with the
thing that exports it. The Linux personality is deliberately *not*
here: it is a compatibility obligation over which the project has no
design authority, its syscall surface is the largest single body of
code in the kernel, and none of it has to be correct for isolation to
hold. That is the whole argument for the boundary sitting where it
does.
Device enumeration is inside; device drivers are not. The kernel walks
ACPI, the device tree and PCI because that needs privilege, then hands
an IoMapping and an IOMMU domain to a ring-3 driver. scripts/
check-device-access.py already holds that seam for the code; this
holds it for the certificate.
Everything the item runs but does not vouch for. A defect here is
bounded by the item's own enforcement: a ring-3 driver fault is a
process fault, and a Linux-personality defect cannot reach an address
space the core did not hand it.
This is not a list of code that matters less. It is the filesystem,
the network stack and the compatibility layer -- most of what makes
Ferrix useful. It is excluded because a claim over 93,714 lines of
product code is a claim nobody can afford to substantiate, and one
over ~40,000 is a claim that can be.

//: Library crates by ring. The rings above classify src/kernel/src file by
file; a crate under src/lib is classified here whole, by its Cargo
package name. Its product code is every file its module tree reaches
from src/lib.rs through declarations not under #[cfg(test)]; a file
reached only through a `#[cfg(test)] mod` is host-test code, counted
apart, and a file under src/ the tree does not reach fails the gate.
The kernel's own packages (kernel_crates below) are not classified here:
they are classified by file, through the rings, each crate holding one
ring's files.
Each entry: `ring` (core, item or load, as for files), `path` (the
crate's directory), and `below` and `above`, the interfaces the crate
meets the rest of the system through, which docs/certification/ITEM.md
section 2 argues. A crate in no entry is unclassified: no item or
core crate may depend on it, and the item-scoped gates do not read it.
The crate-level dependency rule, held by check-item-boundary.py: an
item or core crate's [dependencies] and [build-dependencies], target-
specific ones included, may name only crates of its own ring or one
below it, or a crate in `infrastructure_allowlist`; [dev-dependencies]
are host-test code and are not read. An allowlisted crate's own
dependencies are held to the same rule only once an item crate depends
on it: while none does, an allowlisted crate may gain a load dependency
unremarked. A kernel file naming a crate (`ferrix_btrfs::..`) is
an edge to that crate's ring under dependency_rules, as a `crate::`
path is to a file's.
btrfs joined the item on 2026-10-02 on the customer's decision that it
is certified for as long as it runs inside the kernel. The reader and
the write path are the item; the VFS glue above them is not, because
it is written against the VFS, which is load.

ferrix-btrfs.below: the `Device` trait (ferrix_btrfs::volume::Device): sector reads the kernel's block layer answers (src/kernel/src/fs/btrfs.rs, `Disk`); and caller-lent memory, `ExtentBuffers` and `ChunkStorage`
ferrix-btrfs.above: `Volume` and the on-disk format types it returns (superblock, chunk map, keys, items, the fs and compress modules' readers), called by ferrix-btrfs-write, ferrix-btrfs-vfs and src/kernel/src/fs/btrfs*.rs

ferrix-btrfs-write.below: the `WriteDevice` trait (ferrix_btrfs_write::WriteDevice, a `Device` that also writes and flushes), implemented by the kernel's `Disk`; and ferrix-btrfs, item
ferrix-btrfs-write.above: `WriteVolume` and its transaction, inode and extent operations, called by ferrix-btrfs-vfs and src/kernel/src/fs/btrfs*.rs

ferrix-smbios.below: byte slices its caller lends; no trait, no allocation, no dependency
ferrix-smbios.above: the entry point parse, the table walk and the identity decode, called by src/boot/common/uefi and src/kernel/src/discovery/smbios.rs

ferrix-btrfs-vfs.below: `Volume` and `WriteVolume`, the item's interface above btrfs; it implements `Device` over a cache for them
ferrix-btrfs-vfs.above: ferrix-vfs's `FileSystem` and `Inode`: it is written against the VFS, which is load, and so is load itself

//: Crates an item or core crate may depend on without being classified
itself. Each is no_std infrastructure the core already links and
names from core-ring files; the gate checks that some core or item
kernel file still names it, so an entry cannot outlive that reason.
Being here is not being in the item: the item-scoped gates do not
read these crates. Whether they should be classified `core` is open
(docs/certification/ITEM.md section 2).
infrastructure_allowlist.ferrix-fallible: Fallible Box/Vec/VecDeque/String construction on stable Rust (F-23). The core's own allocation toolkit, src/kernel/src/fallible.rs, is built on it, so an item crate converting to fallible allocation uses the same code the core does rather than a second copy. It also dispatches an item crate's map inserts to the reserved section the kernel installs at boot (set_section, in_section; src/kernel/src/fallible.rs library_section, L.mm.63): ferrix-btrfs-write's every BTreeMap and BTreeSet insert relies on that dispatch to be fallible.
infrastructure_allowlist.ferrix-sync: The spin and sleep locks src/kernel/src/sync.rs wraps for the whole core, and ferrix-fallible's one dependency (its injector's `Once`).

dependency_rules.why: A trusted computing base that reaches upward is not one.
The item may be called by the load above it, and may not call into it. Where it must -- init has to start a filesystem -- the call goes through an interface the item defines, not a module it names.

//: References that break a dependency rule today, each one a finding in
docs/certification/FINDINGS.md. The list exists so the gate can go into
CI green and ratchet down; it is a debt register, not an exemption
mechanism. Every entry needs a finding id, and the gate fails if the
list grows or if an entry goes stale.
Populated by running the gate. An empty list here on a tree that has
never been measured would be a lie told by omission.
Until 2026-09-26 the gate saw only paths written `crate::a::b` in
source whose strings it could not always find, so every count it gave,
from the audit's 62 to the 29 before this note, was a lower bound. The
27 entries added that day were there all along: nested `use` groups,
paths through `use` and sibling `mod` names, and code the old string
pattern had read as a literal (docs/certification/FINDINGS.md, A).
Empty since 2026-09-26, when W-5 closed F-07, F-09 and F-33, the last
three findings with entries here. Empty is a measurement by the
resolving gate, not a default: the list stays, so that a new upward
reference has to be argued into it against a finding, and a closed one
cannot come back unrecorded.
The crate root is in the item ring -- it is bring-up -- and it is also
where the load ring is composed with the item: it tells the load to
register into the item's interfaces (register_load), brings the load's
subsystems up in order, and runs their boot self-checks. Since the kernel
split (docs/KERNEL-CRATES.md, S3) it is the binary's root and declares no
module of the kernel's but stages_check: each crate's root declares its
own, and main.rs reaches them through ferrix_kernel_load, which re-exports
the crates below it. Its references into the load are that
composition, which the item's design asks for, so they are not filed
against a finding. They are listed rather than allowed, and ratcheted
like the debt register: the list may shrink freely, and the gate fails
on a new module or a stale one. What an assessor has to accept is that
these edges carry no item logic; docs/certification/ITEM.md section 2
says why that is plausible and what would make it checkable.
//hooks: Link-time hooks (docs/OPAQUE-KERNEL.md section 9.7, as built, 2 and 3;
the consultant's ledger line 415, H1): a function a core or item file
declares in an `unsafe extern "Rust"` block, defined once in this file
under #[unsafe(no_mangle)] as one call of `forwards_to`. A direct call
up into a ring above, where a registered pointer would be an indirect
one; the core still decides at run time whether to make it, by flags of
its own. check-item-boundary.py fails on a declaration not listed here,
a definition elsewhere or doing more than forwarding, and a stale entry.
//policy: The item's discovery policy the core's device checks are handed through
core may not name discovery::pci or discovery::firmware. check-item-boundary.py
fails a field bound to anything but the path recorded here, a Policy built
anywhere but the composition root, a field not recorded, and a Default.

hooks.name: ferrix_fast_write_read
hooks.why: the x86-64 entry's fast path for channel_write_read, called only while trap::fast_path_on (T1)

hooks.name: ferrix_filter_quiet
hooks.why: T2's quiet predicate, asked by trap::filter_quiet only for a filter registered with it: main.rs's filter_quiet_of_personality, which is syscall::seccomp::quiet with linux_abi=on and false with off, where no filter is registered (LINUX-ABI-SEPARATION.md 11.11)

//: The kernel's Cargo packages and the rings each holds (docs/KERNEL-CRATES.md;
the certification consultant's ledger lines 1477 and 1531). `root` is the
crate root, a file in src/kernel/src beside main.rs; `rings` the rings whose
files the crate's module tree may reach. check-item-boundary.py walks every
root and fails a kernel file reached by no crate or by two, a file in a crate
that does not hold its ring (but for the crate's own root and the entries of
raised_checks), a package under src/kernel missing here, and, for a crate
holding the core or the item alone, a dependency on anything above its ring.
Since the split (step S3) the binary holds only its root, main.rs, the
composition root, and the raised stages_check.rs.
`unclassified_deps` (ledger line 1585, Q1): the libraries a core or item crate
depends on that `crates` does not classify and the allowlist does not hold --
exactly the ones its files name. It is F-76's debt register, not an
endorsement: those crates are linked into the item and no item-scoped gate
reads them. The gate fails an unclassified dependency not listed here, and an
entry the manifest no longer has or no file of the crate names. The list may
shrink freely and grows only with a ledger line; a classified crate of a
higher ring fails whatever this list says.
The four crates build with one build script, src/kernel/build.rs, which makes
the build flags each crate's cfgs and links only the binary (ledger line 3282,
(K1)); check-item-boundary.py fails a kernel crate built with another or none,
and any other package naming it. The core's build_flag_word! is expanded in
each crate and the binary requires the four words equal at compile time (K4).

//: Check files a crate above their ring's builds, because what they check needs
that crate (docs/KERNEL-CRATES.md section 3 (3)): each entry a file matching
test_file_patterns and the crate that reaches it. A ratchet like
known_violations: it may shrink freely; an entry whose file is back in its
ring's crate, or is no kernel file, fails as stale; a product file is never

listed. Filled by the split (step S3): 26 files, each needing the load to run what it checks (stages_check.rs: the binary). `file_ring` is the file's own ring (not `ring`, which names a classified crate's ring to the step cache's reader).
